unit.title: Inside the stock exchange
unit.description: What a stock exchange is, who trades on it, how prices are set and how the Spanish one works

steps.title: An organised market
steps.body:
A **stock exchange** is a regulated market where securities are bought and sold: shares, bonds, ETFs. It brings together people who want to buy and people who want to sell, with the same rules for everyone and public prices.

In Spain it's run by **BME** (Bolsas y Mercados Españoles), part of the Swiss SIX group, and supervised by the **CNMV** (Spain's securities regulator).

steps.title: What it's for
steps.body:
• **For companies:** raising money to grow by selling shares or bonds.
• **For investors:** owning a piece of companies and being able to **sell whenever they want** (liquidity).
• **For everyone:** a public, transparent price for every security at every moment.

steps.title: You don't go to the exchange
steps.body: You buy through an authorised **broker**, who takes your order to the market. And when you buy, someone sells: day to day, the exchange doesn't sell you anything, it just matches orders.
steps.key: The exchange is the meeting point; the broker is the way in.
steps.tip: Every time you buy, someone sells. Ask yourself what they know that you don't.

steps.title: The participants
steps.body:
• **Retail investors:** individuals like you.
• **Institutional investors:** investment funds, pension plans, insurers. They move huge amounts.
• **Market makers:** they always quote a buying price and a selling price and earn the difference.
• **High-frequency traders:** algorithms that trade in microseconds.
• **Central banks and governments**, in bonds and currencies.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body:
On the other side of your order there are usually professionals with more information, better tools and almost zero costs. That's why trying to beat them in the short term is so hard.

In the long term, though, you're not competing with them: you share in what companies earn.

steps.title: Your edge
steps.body: A retail investor doesn't have to report every quarter, can wait for years and can keep costs very low. That's their edge, not speed.
steps.key: The stock market is full of professionals: your edge is time and low costs.
steps.tip: Don't try to outrun an algorithm: you don't need to.

steps.title: The order book
steps.body:
Every security has a book with two columns:

• **Buyers (*bid*):** the best one pays **€10.02** for 500 shares.
• **Sellers (*ask*):** the best one asks **€10.04** for 300 shares; the next, **€10.05** for 800.

The difference between the best *bid* and the best *ask* is the **spread**.

steps.title: How the price moves
steps.body:
If more buyers in a hurry turn up than sellers, they «eat up» the 300 shares at €10.04 and the price climbs to the next step, €10.05. If more sellers turn up, it falls.

News, company results or an economic data release change what people are willing to pay.

steps.title: Auctions
steps.body: The Madrid Stock Exchange opens and closes with an **auction**: from 8:30 to 9:00 and from 17:30 to 17:35 orders build up and a single price is set that matches the largest volume.
steps.key: The price is the latest deal between whoever pays most and whoever asks least.
steps.tip: The price isn't what a company is worth: it's what someone has just paid.

steps.title: When each exchange opens (Spanish mainland time)
steps.body:
• **Madrid, Frankfurt, Paris:** from 9:00 to 17:30.
• **London:** from 8:00 to 16:30 local time = from 9:00 to 17:30 in Spain.
• **New York (NYSE, Nasdaq):** from 9:30 to 16:00 local time = from **15:30 to 22:00** in Spain.
• **Tokyo:** opens in the middle of the night in Spain and takes a lunch break (Tokyo time).

steps.title: Markets that never close
steps.body:
• **Crypto:** 24 hours, 7 days, bank holidays included.
• **Currencies:** 24 hours, from Sunday night to Friday night.

Watch out for the **clock change:** the US and Europe don't change on the same day, so for a few weeks a year New York opens at **14:30** Spanish time.

steps.title: Outside trading hours
steps.body: If you place an order while the exchange is closed, it waits for the open. And whatever happens overnight (results, news) can make the price open far from the previous close: that's a **gap**.
steps.key: Before you trade, check whether the market is open.
steps.tip: Just because the app lets you tap «buy» doesn't mean the market is open.

steps.title: What a broker does
steps.body:
The **broker** receives your order, takes it to the market and charges you fees. In Spain it must be authorised by the **CNMV** or by the regulator of another EU country with a «European passport».

Check on the CNMV website before opening an account.

steps.title: Settlement and custody
steps.body:
Once matched, the trade **settles**: the money goes to the seller and the shares to you. In Europe it takes two business days (**T+2**); in the US, one (T+1) since 2024.

In Spain the central register is **Iberclear**. The **custodian** holds your securities **in your name**, kept separate from the broker's own assets.

steps.title: What if it goes bust?
steps.body: Your shares are still yours. If anything were missing, in Spain the **FOGAIN** (Spain's investor guarantee fund) steps in, up to **€100,000** per investor. With a broker from another EU country, that country's fund covers you, and it may cover less (the EU minimum is €20,000).
steps.key: The broker is your way in; your securities are held in your name.
steps.tip: FOGAIN doesn't cover you if your shares fall: only if the firm can't give you back what's yours.

steps.title: Two markets
steps.body:
• **Primary market:** new securities are **issued** and the issuer receives the money. For example, a stock market listing with new shares or a capital increase.
• **Secondary market:** investors buy and sell securities that already exist among themselves. It's the everyday stock market: the company **gets nothing**.

steps.title: Going public
steps.body:
There are two ways, often combined:

• **OPS (public subscription offer, in Spanish terms):** new shares are created; the money goes to the company.
• **OPV (public sale offer):** the current owners sell some of their shares; the money goes to them.

Internationally it's all called an IPO. Beforehand, the CNMV approves a **prospectus** with the information and the risks.

steps.title: Beware the hype
steps.body: Listings arrive with lots of publicity, but the price is set by whoever's selling, and they know the company better than you do. Many end up trading below their offer price.
steps.key: Primary: the money goes to the issuer. Secondary: it goes to another investor.
steps.tip: If everyone's talking about an IPO, ask yourself who's in a hurry to sell.

u5l7.title: The Spanish stock market: the IBEX and the continuous market

steps.title: The continuous market
steps.body:
Spain's four stock exchanges (Madrid, Barcelona, Bilbao and Valencia) are linked in one electronic system, the **SIBE** or **continuous market**: over a hundred companies trade from 9:00 to 17:30 with a single order book per security.

It's run by **BME**, part of the Swiss SIX group since 2020.

steps.title: The IBEX 35
steps.body:
It brings together the **35 most liquid companies** on the continuous market, weighted by market capitalisation (counting only freely traded shares). A technical committee reviews it twice a year, in June and December: some companies come in and others drop out.

Its base was **3,000 points** at the end of 1989.

steps.title: Other segments
steps.body:
• **BME Growth:** small, expanding companies, with fewer requirements and more risk (formerly MAB).
• **Latibex:** Latin American companies trading in euros.
• **Fixed income:** bonds and bills.
steps.key: The IBEX 35 is the shop window; the continuous market is the whole shop.
steps.tip: Not being in the IBEX doesn't make it a bad company: it just means it's traded less.
